title: Effectiveness of Some 0 dB Cryogenic Microwave Attenuators as Thermal Heatsinks
authors: J. T. Klomp, Haoyun Huang, G. A. Csathy
abstract: Coaxial cables are widely used in radiofrequency and microwave cryogenic setups for condensed matter and quantum experiments. Since the inner conductor of coaxes is often in good thermal contact with the sample to be measured, it is desirable to know the phononic heat channeled by the inner conductor. Although cryogenic attenuators are widely used to thermalize the inner conductor of coaxes, to our knowledge, quantitative information is not available. We present data on the effectiveness of three commercially available 0 dB attenuators as thermal heatsinks. In particular, we measured the temperature of the inner pin of several 0 dB attenuators under a heat load. This information will aid in designing and carefully controlling the thermal environment of samples in high-frequency experiments mounted in dilution refrigerators and on nuclear demagnetization stages.
summary: This experimental paper characterizes how effectively different commercial cryogenic microwave attenuators function as thermal heatsinks. By measuring their temperature response under controlled heat loads, the authors provide quantitative data on their thermal transresistance and time constants. This information is vital for designing reliable and accurately controlled thermal environments in advanced low-temperature quantum experiments.
main_problem: The study aims to quantify the thermal performance of cryogenic microwave attenuators when used as thermal anchors for coaxial cables in ultra-low temperature quantum experiments.
main_result: The quartz crystal attenuator was found to be significantly more effective than teflon or sealed alternatives, providing better thermal anchoring and lower thermal transresistance at various temperatures.
method: The authors measured the temperature response of three different commercial 0 dB attenuators by applying controlled heat loads and measuring the resulting temperature change versus applied power.
model_or_system: The physical system involves coaxial cables used in dilution refrigerators, focusing on the thermal coupling through the inner conductor. The measurement characterizes the attenuator's ability to act as a reliable thermal heatsink.
key_observables: Thermal transresistance (R), temperature dependence of R, and thermal equilibration time constant ($\tau$).
important_parameters: Operating temperatures in the millikelvin range ($T_{mx}$), applied heating power ($P$), and material types (quartz crystal vs. teflon).
main_assumptions: The body of the attenuator is assumed to be in strong thermal contact with the mixing chamber, and comparisons are made between different thermal models (e.g., simple resistance vs. distributed resistance).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, show temperature readings versus applied power for a specific attenuator, plot thermal response curves and transresistance across various base temperatures, and compare temporal decay rates ($\tau$) for different materials.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the need for accurate thermal characterization in cryogenic setups, details the measurement methodology using three distinct attenuators, presents quantitative results comparing their performance metrics (R and $\tau$), and concludes with guidelines for designing better thermal environments.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum dynamics, understanding the precise thermal environment is crucial for any experiment involving sensitive quantum devices (like qubits or superconducting circuits) where temperature fluctuations can cause decoherence or measurement errors.
